blocks.text: ونهار رايت نصف ليل [wa-nahār raʾaytu niṣfa layl] ✡ وليل رايت وسط النهار [wa-layl raʾaytu wasaṭa al-nahār] ✡ [III, 28] In these lines he seems to say that he saw day at midnight and night at midday, whereas there نهار [nahār] and ليل [layl] do not mean day and night, but the young of the bustard and of the partridge. I could add many things of this kind, drawn from Abenbitar, Damir and Alkazuinius, if this were the matter at hand; but it will suffice to have observed that in the description of this bird there is one point on which the Arabs are διαῤῥήδην [diarrhēdēn] opposed to the Greeks. For the Greeks assert [col. 284] that it has a short and slow flight because of the heaviness of its body. Xenoph. in the Cyrus the Younger, book 1: Τὰς δ᾽ ὠτίδας, ἄν τις ταχὺ ἀνίστῃ, ἔστι λαμβάνειν· πέτονται γὰρ βραχὺ, ὥσπερ πέρδικες, καὶ ταχὺ ἀπαγορεύουσι [Tas d᾽ ōtidas, an tis tachy anistē, esti lambanein; petontai gar brachy, hōsper perdikes, kai tachy apagoreuousi]. Bustards, however, can be caught if one presses them hard: for they fly only a little, like partridges, and quickly tire. And Athenaeus, in book 9, on this passage of Xenophon: Ἀληθῆ λέγειν φησὶ τὸν Ξενοφῶντα ὁ Πλούταρχος περὶ τῶν ὠτίδων [Alēthē legein phēsi ton Xenophōnta ho Ploutarchos peri tōn ōtidōn]; Plutarch reports that Xenophon told the truth about bustards. Aelian, book 5, chapter 24: Of birds, bustards alone fear dogs; τὸ αἴτιον, βαρεῖαί τε εἰσι, καὶ σαρμῶν (read σαρκῶν) ὄγκον περιφέρουσιν [to aition, bareiai te eisi, kai sarmōn (sarkōn) onkon peripherousin], because they are heavy and carry about a mass of flesh. And so their wings do not easily raise and lift them. Hence, burdened by the bulk of their body, they fly low and near the ground, and are often caught by dogs. And for this very reason they seem to have been called tardae [slow]. Pliny, book 10, chapter 22: Next to them (the ostriches) are the birds which Spain calls aves tardas, and Greece otides. The old Glosses: Avis tarda, ὦτος [ōtos]; read ὠτίς [ōtis]. For the otus is another bird. The Glosses of Philoxenus: Ὠτὶς τὸ ὄρνεον [Ōtis to orneon], Avis tarda. Accordingly the Spaniards still today call them abestardas, as we call them oustardas. Yet the Arabs actually praise them for their flight. Damir: وهي من اشد الطير طيرانا وابعدها سوطا وذلك انها تصاد بالبصرة فيوجد في حواصلها الحبة الخضر التي شجرها البطم ومنابتها في تخوم ارض الشام ولذلك قالوا في المثل اطير من الحباري [wa-hiya min ashadd al-ṭayr ṭayarānan wa-abʿadihā sawṭan wa-dhālika annahā tuṣād bi-l-Baṣra fa-yūjad fī ḥawāṣilihā al-ḥabba al-khaḍr allatī shajaruhā al-buṭm wa-manābituhā fī tukhūm arḍ al-Shām wa-li-dhālika qālū fī al-mathal aṭyar min al-ḥubārā] That the bird has a very strong flight and roams very far is clear from this: when it is caught around Basra (at the mouth of the Euphrates), a green seed is found in its crop, whose tree, the terebinth, grows in the borders of Damascene Syria. Hence we say in a common proverb that someone is „more volatile than the bustard,“ if the word may be pardoned ^{(7)}.

[III, 29] Further, of so many versions of the word ינשוף jansuph I prefer the Syriac and the Chaldee, in which it is rendered קפופא kiphupha, that is, eagle owl. For it is agreed that ינשוף jansuph is derived from the Hebrew נשף neseph, which means twilight and darkness. From this it is inferred, on very probable grounds, that this bird is nocturnal. Thus in Arabic, in Alcamus, رامسات [rāmisāt] ramisath are birds that fly by night, الطير التي تطير بالليل [al-ṭayr allatī taṭīr bi-l-layl], because for the Chaldeans and Syrians ܪܡܫܐ ramsa is evening. And Es. XXXIV, 11. it belongs to the desolation of Idumaea not that the ibis, or the hawk, or the bustard, but that the eagle owl should dwell in it; of which Pliny, book 10, chapter 12: It inhabits deserts, and not only desolate places but also dreadful and inaccessible ones, a monster of the night. And Festus: The buzzard is a cause of desolation to those places which it has entered, like the eagle owl. And the same bird is rightly joined with the raven, since both birds are funereal and of ill omen, and have something dreadful and ominous in their voice. Accordingly Pliny has an entire chapter On birds of ill omen: the crow, ravens, the eagle owl. There he says of the crow, It is itself a bird of ill-omened garrulity. And of the raven, Their worst omen is when they swallow their voice, as if strangled. And of the eagle owl, The eagle owl is funereal, and most abominated in public auspices, etc. Nor is it vocal with any song, but with a groan. And so, if seen in cities or by daylight, it is an altogether dreadful portent. Hence Ovid, Metamorphoses book 5, Fable 8, on Ascalaphus, [col. 285]
He becomes a loathsome bird, the herald of coming grief, the sluggish eagle owl, a dire omen for mortals.
— — — thrice the funereal eagle owl gave an omen with its deadly song.
In a thousand places the Stygian eagle owl gave gloomy omens,
And alone on the rooftops the eagle owl with funereal song was seen to lament. — —
And the nocturnal screech owls groan, and the eagle owl sings of deadly losses. — —
Here the vulture, there the grief-bringing eagle owl groans.
And the author of the Philomela, [III, 30] The eagle owl hoots horribly with funereal song.
